In this week, you will be using your laptops to work with a relatively big research dataset to answer actual research questions that arose from a research project.

## Session's goals

1.  Familiarise with the dataset (and the process it represents)
2.  learn [tidyverse](https://tidyverse.org/)'s syntax for frequent data manipulations:
    1.  `filter()` to subset rows matching some conditions
    2.  `select()`, to subset columns (by name or position)
    3.  `group()` and `summarise()` to compute summaries based on some criteria
    4.  `join_by()` to combine datasets
3.  learn when to apply these methods to address research questions

## The data

The data consists of two `csv` files:

1.  `proposals.csv`: containing all Approved, Rejected and Proposed tagging proposals from the [OSM Wiki](https://wiki.openstreetmap.org), as well as their associated metadata.

2.  `proposals_votes.csv`: containing all the votes cast for every tagging proposal in `proposals`.

Both files were generated using a dedicated R-package called [`{OSMproposals}`](https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/) [@cámara-menoyo2026] which provides reproducible datasets containing information about [OpenStreetMap](http://openstreetmap.org)’s tagging proposals. It does so by querying and webscrapping OSM’s wiki via helper functions. Refer to the official documentation page: <https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/> to see metadata and the source code that generated each dataset.

::: callout-warning
## Important considerations

1.  The provided datasets contain experimental versions of the actual datasets provided by the package, so documentation may slightly differ.
2.  These datasets are part of an ongoing research. **Please, do not share them beyond the classroom unless with explicit permission from their authors.**
:::

### Loading data

The data is provided by you in a folder `data/raw/`. It is a good practice to separate raw data (e.g. extracted from a package, survey...) from final data derived from code calculations. Final data can always be regenerated programmatically, whereas raw data can't.

```{webr urls}
#| warning: false
#| edit: false
#| rownumber: true
library(dplyr)

# We store paths in a variable.
path_proposals <- "data/raw/proposals.csv"
path_votes <- "data/raw/proposals_votes.csv"

```

Load the two datasets and assign them, respectively, to the variables `proposals` and `votes`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_load_data
proposals <- read.csv(______)
______ <- read.csv(______)
```

```{webr}
#| echo: false
proposals <- read.csv(path_proposals) |> 
  as_tibble()
proposals_votes <- read.csv(path_votes) |> 
  as_tibble()
```

### Fixing data

To fix the problem we detected, we need to change `draft_started` column type to a date, and we will be using `mutate()` to do so.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_to_date
proposals <- mutate(proposals, draft_started = as.Date(______))

# Check what we did
glimpse(proposals)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="ex_to_date"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

We are looking for a column name here. We need to write the name of the column that we want to convert to a date.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="ex_to_date"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution:

``` r
proposals <- mutate(proposals, draft_started = as.Date(draft_started))
```
:::
::::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_to_date
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this_code()
```

::: callout-tip
Note that this syntax would be equivalent to base R's syntax:

``` r
proposals$draft_started <- as.Date(proposals$draft_started)
```

At this moment tidyverse syntax may seem a little bit confusing and not very useful, but maybe the next bits can change our minds.
:::

```{webr}
# We can change multiple columns with mutate
proposals <- mutate(
  proposals, 
  draft_started = as.Date(draft_started),
  rfc_start = as.Date(rfc_start),
  vote_start = as.Date(vote_start),
  vote_end = as.Date(vote_end)
)

glimpse(proposals)
```

But actually, it's more common to write this code using the **pipe operator**[^1] `|>`:

[^1]: This operator allows for chaining multiple operations together, streamlining code.\
    The pipe operator (`|>`) takes the value of its left-hand side to the first argument of the function on its right-hand side. This enables a natural and readable way of chaining multiple functions together, reducing the need for intermediate variables and improving code clarity.

    ```{r}
    # Nested, reads inside-out
    round(mean(log(c(10, 100, 1000))), 2)

    # Piped, reads left to right
    c(10, 100, 1000) |> log() |> mean() |> round(2)
    ```

```{webr}
# This is equivalent:
proposals <- proposals |> 
  mutate(
    draft_started = as.Date(draft_started),
    rfc_start = as.Date(rfc_start),
    vote_start = as.Date(vote_start),
    vote_end = as.Date(vote_end)
  )
  
glimpse(proposals)
```

::: callout-important
Bear with me: we will see why this syntax using the pipe operator `|>` is very convenient.
:::

## Answering questions through data

### How diverse are the proposals?

On week 5 [@uprichard2026], we saw the importance of measurments and how deciding what and how to measure is anything but trivial. There are many ways to define diversity. In this case, we will use the language in which the proposals are written as a proxy for diversity.

We are going to use dplyr's `count()` to count the number of different languages used in the column `language`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count_lang
proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(______) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex_count_lang" }
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count_lang
#| solution: true
proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang
```
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_count_lang
#| check: true
gradethis::grade_this_code()
```

`count()` conveniently can sort the values by number of uses:

```{webr}
proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language, sort = TRUE)

proposals_lang
```

::: callout-caution
#### Question: 

What does that information tell us? How is it related to diversity?
:::

### How much labour is required to make a proposal?

Again, there are multiple ways to define labour. One way could be to count **time spent since their initial draft until the end of the voting process**.

::: callout-important
Only a subset of proposals ever get to get voted, so we are going to use `filter()` to **subset** those proposals whose status is either `Approved` or `Rejected` and only `select()` the columns that are needed.
:::

Here, we will be using `select()` to subset **columns**:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_select

# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, ______, ______, ______)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)

```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_select
#| solution: true

# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)

```

And now, let's use `filter()` to subset **rows** whose status is either "Approved" or "Rejected":

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_subset_filter
# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", _______))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_subset_filter
#| solution: true
# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected"))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)
```

```{webr}
head(time_spent_completed)
```

And now, we are going to compute the amount of time spent. We will be using `mutate()` to create a new variable called `time_spent` which is the time difference between the proposal was voted (finished) and drafted (started).

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_time_spent
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = ______ )
  
time_spent_completed
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_time_spent
#| solution: true
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)
  
time_spent_completed
```

::: callout-tip
Remember when we spoke about the pipe operator `|>` ? We could pipe those two verbs in a single expression!

```{webr}
# Pipe multiple verbs into a single expression:
time_spent_completed_piped <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end) |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected")) |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)

# Let's see if these two dataframes are identical:
all.equal(time_spent_completed, time_spent_completed_piped)
```
:::

This new column `time_spent` says how much time each proposal took, in days[^2]. We would need to have some nice summary statistics to have a good overview of the process.

[^2]: Can you edit the code in the cell above to check `time_spent` data type? Is this what you would have expected?

```{webr}
summary(time_spent_completed$time_spent)
```

::: callout-warning
We have some results that are either missing (`NA`) or negative values. This is because either the `draft_started` or `vote_end` values are missing. We should get rid of them to before proceeding.
:::

But what if we wanted to see if there are differences between *approved* and *rejected* proposals? We will use **group_by()** to group by a variable and **summarise()**. to create new summary columns using some statistical functions:

```{webr}
time_spent_completed_summaries <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(time_spent > 0) |> 
  group_by(status_raw) |> 
  summarise(
    min = min(time_spent),
    first_q = quantile(time_spent, probs = 0.25),
    median = median(time_spent),
    mean = mean(time_spent),
    third_q = quantile(time_spent, probs = 0.75),
    max = max(time_spent)
  )

# Do we spot differences between these two groups?
time_spent_completed_summaries
```

::: callout-caution
#### Your turn

Can you think of another variable we could use for measuring the labour involved? Could you do a similar process with this new variable?
:::

### How many votes did each proposal receive?

Votes are stored in a separate dataset `proposals_votes`, so let's do some initial exploration

```{webr}
head(proposals_votes)
```

::: callout-important
#### Wide vs long data[^3]

`proposals_votes` is a **long dataset** (as opposed to a wide one, like the previous one):

- **wide datasets**: each row is an observation, refers to a unique value

- **long dataset**: multiple rows refer to a same observation
:::

[^3]: For a more detailed explanation refer to <https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/tidy-data.html>

We could use what we've learnt to **count** the votes for each proposal and type of vote being cast:

```{webr}
proposals_votes_count_long <- proposals_votes |> 
  count(url, vote)

head(proposals_votes_count_long, 10)
```

We can remove the proposals with no votes:

```{webr}
# Subset rows where vote is not empty.
proposals_votes_count_long <- proposals_votes_count_long |> 
  filter(!is.na(vote)) 
  
head(proposals_votes_count_long, 10)
```

#### Reshaping dataframes

This format is not very useful for us now. It would be better to see how many votes of each type a proposal has received. In other words, we need to convert from a long format to a wide format. To do so, we will use another package from the tidyverse: [`{tidyr}`](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/) provides two convenient functions `pivot_wider()`[^4] to convert from long to wide, and `pivot_longer()`, to do the opposite.

[^4]: This function is full of nuances and requires having a clear picture of the actual data and what the shape we want it to have. Refer to the vignette `vignette::pivot_wider` or the help function `?pivot_wider`

```{webr}
# Uncomment below if you need to install the package:
# install.packages("tidyr")

proposals_votes_count <-  proposals_votes_count_long |> 
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = vote, values_from = n)

head(proposals_votes_count)

```

#### Combining dataframes

We have two datasets: one containing proposals, and another one containing votes. Wouldn't it be nice to have the total votes per proposal in a single dataset?

To combine proposals with `proposals_votes`, we need to:

1.  Make sure that both dataframes have a shared field to use as an index

2.  Make sure that both dataframes are either long or wide

Gladly, both conditions are met, so we are ready to join them.

```{webr}
proposals <- proposals |> 
  left_join(votes_count, by = join_by(fullurl == url))
```

#### Piping everything

Or, we could do all of this (and something more) piping multiple verbs in one statement:

```{webr}
# Doing everything at one go
votes_count <- proposals_votes |>
  filter(!is.na(vote)) |>
  count(url, vote) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = vote, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    votes_total = rowSums(
      across(c(Approve, Oppose, Abstain, Other)),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  rename(
    votes_approve = Approve,
    votes_oppose = Oppose,
    votes_abstain = Abstain,
    votes_other = Other
  )

proposals <- proposals |> 
  # Incorporate votes
  left_join(votes_count, by = join_by(fullurl == url))

```

::: callout-caution
#### Question

Can you guess what additional steps did we do and what are their outcomes?
:::

## Further questions

By now, you should be equipped to answer the following questions by adapting the code above:

1.  What gets proposed?
2.  What's the general outcome of the tagging proposal?
3.  What are the more controversial proposals?

And questions related to measurement:

1.  Has this process or its outcomes changed over time?
2.  How can we operationalise diversity?
